newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr deadlocked, govt review no help.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr deadlocked, govt review no help.

text.p: The Australian dollar remained locked in a tight, tense standoff with its U.S. counterpart Tuesday, but did make up ground on most crosses.

The market showed scant immediate reaction to the government's mid-year economic review in which forecasts for 1996/97 inflation were lowered while GDP growth remained the same at 3.5 percent. This was much as expected, but the estimate for the budget deficit was revised to a wider than expected A$8.5 billion, which could bruise offshore sentiment.
Overall, however, analysts saw little in the review to change market thinking on interest rate, and so the dollar.

"The deficit is a bit of a problem and might have some effect at the margin for policy, but it won't be a central concern of the RBA," said Peter Munckton, senior economist at Bankers Trust Australia.

The market seemed to agree and left the dollar idle at US$0.7730/35 by 4.30 pm (0530 GMT) from an early US$0.7721/26 and a matching US$0.7730/35 late here Friday ahead of the Australia Day holiday weekend.
Dealers said volumes had been very light and trading ranges were well defined by corporate and U.S. investment bank bids at 77 cents and a wall of offshore offers at US$0.7745 resistance.

The local dollar showed more direction on the crosses where the European currencies and the yen were under pressure from expectations that interest rates will remain low or even ease again in many of the countries concerned.
A noteable casualty was the Swiss franc which tumbled when Swiss finance minister Kaspar Villiger said he was relieved at the currency's recent decline.

That reinforced the message of the Swiss central bank, which has been talking the franc down for some time, and boosted the dollar close to 4-1/2 year highs at 1.1101/14 francs from 1.1032/48 late Monday.

The local currency held firm on the yen for most of the session but edged back to 92.66/76 in late trade, from 92.73/83 late Friday, when rumours circulated that the Bank of Japan was checking rates on US$/yen as a prelude to intervening.
The U.S. unit had been probing the psychologically important 120.00 yen level at the time and the market was concerned it might have risen too fast for the BOJ's comfort.
The gains on the crosses were still enough to lift the Australian dollar 0.3 point on its trade weighted index to 58.8.
The only domestic news was the government's review and most of the economic projections in it were predictable.
"The economic forecasts were in line with what we looked for and should not have surprised anyone," said Munckton at BT.
Crucially, the key underlying measure of inflation was now expected to average 2.0 percent in 1996/97 against 2.75 percent at the time of the budget in August.

That outlook should be backed up by the December quarter inflation figures due Wednesday which are widely expected to show the underlying measure slowed to 2.1 percent annual growth from 2.4 percent in Q3. While a lower result would reignite talk of an imminent rate cut and likely depress the dollar, analysts were not so sure inflation alone would tip the RBA's hand.
"The outlook on prices is good, but we reckon that's already been reflected in the 150 basis points of easing already undertaken," said Munckton.
"I think the RBA will need to see more weakness in the real economy to move again, and that probably means no cut at the February board meeting."

The market would have to suffer until February 5 -- the day after the meeting -- to know if that view was correct, but if rates were held a short covering rally to 78 cents was more than possible, dealers said.
